case.dispatchHook: Motion alert at the St. Petersburg pier! Mystery forces are moving things around.
briefing: Agent, strange motion reports are rolling in from the St. Petersburg pier!
A snack cart rolled away, a runaway bike zoomed past, and a coconut dropped.
Sort each motion card by the force behind it, then track down the speed logs.
Grab your force sensor and let's find out what got everything moving!

lab.intro: Mystery motions are happening all over the pier! Sort each card into the bin for the force that caused it.

bins.name: Push or pull
bins.hint: Something touches an object to push it away or pull it closer.

bins.name: Gravity
bins.hint: Earth pulls objects straight down toward the ground without touching them.

bins.name: Friction
bins.hint: Surfaces rub together and resist motion to slow things down.

bins.name: Magnetic force
bins.hint: A magnet pushes or pulls another magnet, or pulls on iron or steel, without touching.

cards.name: Soccer kick
card: A foot hits a soccer ball.
The ball flies across the field.
cards.why: Spot on! The foot makes contact with the ball and pushes it across the field.

cards.name: Wagon of oranges
card: Agent Rosa grabs the wagon handle.
She walks forward and the wagon rolls behind her.
cards.why: You got it! Pulling the wagon handle moves the wagon forward behind Rosa.

cards.name: Coconut drop
card: A coconut comes loose from a palm tree.
Nothing touches it on the way down to the sand.
cards.why: Spot on! Gravity pulls the coconut down toward Earth without touching it.

cards.name: Afternoon storm
card: Raindrops form in a Florida cloud.
They fall to the street below.
cards.why: You got it! Gravity pulls the raindrops straight down from the sky to the ground.

cards.name: Bike brakes
card: Rubber pads squeeze the spinning bike wheel.
The bike slows down and stops.
cards.why: Spot on! The brake pads rub against the spinning wheel, creating friction that slows the bike down.

cards.name: Book on carpet
card: Agent Kai slides a book across the carpet.
The book slows and stops after a short slide.
cards.why: You got it! Friction between the rough carpet and the sliding book slows the book down.

cards.name: Toy train cars
card: The front of a toy train car comes near another car.
They snap together before they even touch.
cards.why: Spot on! Magnetic force pulls the train cars together without needing to touch first.

cards.name: Spilled pins
card: Agent Sam holds a gray bar magnet over steel pins and wooden beads.
The steel pins jump right up, but the wooden beads stay put.
cards.why: You got it! The magnet pulls on steel objects without touching them, but it does not pull on wood.

case.debriefClosed: Awesome job, Agent! Every mystery motion on the pier is solved, and each force is logged correctly.
case.debriefOpen: This case stays open for now, Agent. Check the pier cargo scales and come back soon to test more forces!

items.stem: Agent Maya watches a ripe apple break from a tree branch. The apple falls to the ground. Next, a ball thrown straight up slows, stops, and comes back down. Which force pulls both objects down?
options: friction
magnetic force
gravity
a push from the air
why: Friction happens when surfaces rub together to resist motion. It does not pull objects down.
Magnetic force pulls on metals like iron and steel. It does not pull apples or rubber balls.
Spot on! Earth's gravity pulls objects straight toward the ground without even touching them.
Air can resist falling objects and slow them down, but air does not pull objects down toward Earth.
items.alt: An apple falling from a tree with a downward arrow, and a ball thrown up arcing back down.
items.tisCheck: Gravity acting on falling objects; forces limited to pushes, pulls, friction, gravity and magnetic force.
items.misconceptions: Air thought to push things down; gravity thought to need contact.

items.stem: Four remote-control boats each crossed the same 20 m pool. Agent Leo timed each boat with a stopwatch. Which boat was the fastest?
options: Boat 1
Boat 2
Boat 3
Boat 4
why: Check the timer column! Boat 1 took 8 seconds, which is longer than Boat 4's 5 seconds.
Watch out for big numbers! A time of 12 seconds means Boat 2 took the longest to finish, making it the slowest boat.
Take another look at the times! Boat 3 took 10 seconds, which is slower than Boat 4.
Spot on! Every boat crossed the same 20 meters. The boat with the shortest time, 5 seconds, was the fastest!
items.alt: A table showing four boats that each crossed 20 m: Boat 1 in 8 seconds, Boat 2 in 12 seconds, Boat 3 in 10 seconds and Boat 4 in 5 seconds.
items.tisCheck: Speed as distance in a unit of time (SC.4.P.12.2), read from a table by comparing; no computation.
items.misconceptions: The biggest number in the table taken as the fastest; time and speed confused.

items.stem: Agent Kai tracks how far Jo and Sam walked along the St. Petersburg pier over the same amount of time. Jo's line is steeper than Sam's line. Which statement is supported by the graph?
options: Jo walked faster, because Jo covered more distance in the same time.
Sam walked faster, because Sam's line is less steep.
They walked at the same speed, because they walked for the same amount of time.
Jo walked slower, because a steep line means walking uphill.
why: Spot on! On a distance and time graph, a steeper line means covering more distance in the same time. Jo walked faster!
Check the slope again! A flatter, less steep line means Sam covered less distance in that time, so Sam was slower.
Look at the distance axis! Even though both walked for the same time, Jo traveled much farther down the pier.
Keep in mind what the graph tracks! The graph compares distance and time, not hills. A steep line means higher speed.
items.alt: A distance and time line graph with two lines, a steep line for Jo and a shallow line for Sam.
items.tisCheck: Speed read from a distance and time graph (SC.4.P.12.2); conceptual only, no computation.
items.misconceptions: A graph read as a picture of a hill; the same time taken to mean the same speed.

items.stem: Agent Elena and Agent Marcus give the same empty cart a light push, a medium push, and a hard push on the same smooth floor. They measure how far the cart rolls each time. Which statement is supported by the data?
options: A lighter push makes the cart roll farther.
A harder push makes the cart roll farther.
The cart rolls the same distance no matter how hard the push.
The cart rolls farther because the floor is smooth, not because of the push.
why: Check the table row for the light push! It only moved the cart 1 meter, which was the shortest distance of all.
Spot on! A bigger push causes a bigger change in motion. The hard push sent the cart rolling 6 meters!
Look at the distance column! The cart rolled 1 meter, 3 meters, and 6 meters, so the distances were different.
Remember what stayed the same! The floor was smooth for every push, so the force of each push made the difference.
items.alt: A table showing the cart rolled 1 m after a light push, 3 m after a medium push and 6 m after a hard push.
items.tisCheck: A greater push causes a greater change in motion (SC.5.P.13.2); comparing values only, no computation.
items.misconceptions: The size of a push not linked to motion; a condition held the same (the floor) credited for the change.

items.stem: Agent Maya gives the same toy car the same push on two tracks. The car rolls far on the smooth tile track. It stops much sooner on the carpet track. Why does the car stop sooner on the carpet?
options: The carpet has more friction, which resists the car's motion.
The carpet has less friction, which slows the car down.
Gravity is stronger on the carpet.
The tile track pushes the car forward.
why: Spot on! Rough surfaces like carpet produce more friction, which resists the rolling wheels and stops the car sooner.
Think about sliding surfaces! Less friction lets objects glide farther. More friction is what brings things to a stop.
Gravity pulls downward with the exact same strength on both tracks. Surface texture is what changed here.
Surfaces do not push rolling cars forward. The smooth tile simply has very little friction to slow the car down.
items.alt: The same toy car on a smooth tile track and on a carpet track, traveling a shorter distance on the carpet.
items.tisCheck: Friction only as resistance to movement; forces limited to pushes, pulls, friction, gravity and magnetic force.
items.misconceptions: Friction thought to push things or to belong to smooth surfaces; gravity thought to change with the surface.

items.stem: Agent Rosa tests two bar magnets in her lab kit. When the north pole of one faces the south pole of the other, they pull together. When two north poles face each other, they push apart. What will happen when she turns the magnets so two south poles face each other?
options: They pull together, because all magnet ends attract each other.
Nothing happens, because the magnets are not touching.
They stick together, because magnets attract any metal.
They push apart, because like poles repel.
why: Check the north poles rule! Two north poles pushed apart, so magnet ends do not always attract each other.
Remember how magnets work! Magnetic force acts across space without touching, just like the north poles did.
Look closely at the poles! While magnets attract iron and steel, two matching magnet poles push away from each other.
You got it! Two south poles are like poles. Just like two north poles, like poles push apart and repel!
keyWords: north pole of one faces the south pole
two south poles face each other
items.alt: Two bar magnets with north facing south pulling together, and two bar magnets with north facing north pushing apart.
items.tisCheck: Magnetic attraction and repulsion as a force that can act without touching; no field lines.
items.misconceptions: All magnet ends thought to attract; magnetic force thought to need contact.

items.stem: Two field teams play tug-of-war on the beach at Fort De Soto. The table shows how many agents are on each team and how hard each team pulls. Which way will the rope move?
options: toward the right team, because it has more agents
toward the left team, because it pulls harder
nowhere, because both teams are pulling
toward the right team, because the rope moves away from the harder pull
why: Look at how hard each team pulls! Player count does not decide it because the left team pulls with more force.
Spot on! When two pulls are unequal, an object moves toward the stronger pull. The left team pulls harder!
Check the balance of forces! The rope only stays still if both pulls are equal. Here, one team pulls much harder.
Think about how pulling works! When a team pulls an object with greater force, the object moves toward them, not away.
keyWords: Which way will the rope move
items.alt: A table showing the left team has 4 agents pulling strong and the right team has 5 agents pulling weak.
items.tisCheck: Unequal pulls change an object's motion; described as pulls only, with no term for combined forces.
items.misconceptions: More people thought to always win; any two pulls thought to cancel.

items.stem: Agent Sam tracked a gentle manatee swimming in Tampa Bay. The table shows how far it was from the dock each minute. Which statement describes the manatee's motion?
options: It sped up, because the numbers get bigger each minute.
It slowed down each minute.
It swam the same distance each minute, so its speed stayed the same.
It swam 150 m every minute.
why: Look at how much distance was added each minute! The total grew, but it moved exactly 50 meters every single minute.
Check the rate of change! The manatee traveled 50 meters between minutes 1 and 2, and another 50 meters in minute 3.
Spot on! The manatee swam exactly 50 meters during each single minute, so its speed stayed the same.
Check the total time! The manatee was 150 meters out after 3 full minutes, not in one single minute.
keyWords: how far it was from the dock each minute
items.alt: A table showing the manatee was 0 m from the dock at 0 minutes, 50 m at 1 minute, 100 m at 2 minutes and 150 m at 3 minutes.
items.tisCheck: Speed as distance in a unit of time read from a table (SC.4.P.12.2); equal steps of 50 are read as a pattern, no computation is required.
items.misconceptions: Growing totals read as speeding up; total distance mistaken for distance in each minute.

codex.title: Gravity
codex.line: Gravity pulls objects toward Earth, even when nothing touches them.

codex.title: Friction
codex.line: Friction is a force that resists motion when two surfaces rub together.

codex.title: Magnetic force
codex.line: Magnets attract iron and steel, and two like poles of magnets push apart.
